# Problemset TeacherGradingBias

```{r 'check_ps', include=FALSE}

user.name = ''
```


## Exercise 1 -- Overview and Motivation

### Overview

This interactive problem set is part of my bachelor’s thesis at Ulm University. It reproduces and discusses the empirical strategy of Botelho, Madeira, and Rangel (2015), who study whether Black students in São Paulo receive lower teacher-assigned mathematics grades than comparable White classmates. The article page and the replication materials are available [here](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/app.20140352).

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run for additional info in the Viewer pane
info("Note - Links & Navigation")
```

The empirical setting combines administrative data from São Paulo on eighth-grade students, their backgrounds, classrooms, and teachers with two measures of performance for the same students: teacher-assigned mathematics grades and blindly scored standardized mathematics tests. This distinction between classroom grades and external test scores is the empirical core of the problem set. It allows us to compare teacher-mediated assessment with an external achievement benchmark.

The problem set proceeds in stages. It first introduces the data and descriptive patterns, then moves to within-classroom comparisons, richer control sets, proxy variables for behavior and effort, measurement-error concerns, fixed-effects instrumental-variable specifications, alternative teacher-assigned outcomes, teacher heterogeneity, and repeated teacher-student interaction. The purpose is not only to reproduce empirical results, but to understand what each specification can and cannot establish.

### How to work on the problem set

The problem set is designed as a guided investigation. The exercises should therefore be completed in order. However, it is also possible to work on each exercise independently, because every exercise reloads the objects needed. Within each exercise, tasks should be solved sequentially.

You will encounter three main types of code chunks:

* chunks where you write the solution yourself,
* chunks with gaps where you replace `___`,
* chunks with ready-to-run code that you only need to check.

If you want to work on a chunk, click `edit` first. If you need support, click `hint`. If you want to see the correct solution, use `solution`. If you want to run code without checking it, click `run`. To verify your answer, click `check`.

In addition to code tasks, the problem set also contains quizzes. Some of them are simple comprehension checks, while others are designed to deepen your understanding of the paper’s methods and findings.

Once you have completed a section, click `Go to next exercise...` to continue.

### Motivation and research question

Grades matter because they are more than classroom records. They document academic performance, shape how students are evaluated by schools, and may affect access to later educational opportunities. In the setting studied by Botelho et al. (2015), teacher-assigned grades enter consequential school evaluations, including promotion and retention decisions. More generally, recent evidence suggests that Grade Point Average (GPA) can affect later educational and labor-market trajectories. Using Norwegian administrative data, Landaud et al. (2026) show that a higher high-school GPA improves access to a broader and more selective set of higher education programs and leads to persistent gains in later labor-market outcomes, especially wages.

At the same time, teacher-assigned grades are not purely mechanical achievement measures. They are produced inside an institutional relationship between teachers and students. They may reflect test performance and subject proficiency, but also participation, classroom behavior, homework, effort, and other information observed during the school year. This creates scope for subjective or teacher-mediated assessment. A related literature therefore studies whether evaluations differ when performance is assessed by teachers rather than externally or blindly. For example, Hanna and Linden (2012) experimentally study discrimination in grading by randomly assigning student characteristics to exam cover sheets. Their design illustrates why the distinction between externally measured achievement and teacher-mediated evaluation is empirically important.

Botelho et al. (2015) contribute to this literature by comparing teacher-assigned mathematics grades with blindly scored standardized mathematics tests for the same students. Teacher-assigned grades are internal evaluations made by teachers during the school year. Blindly scored standardized tests, by contrast, provide an external reference of proficiency that is not directly determined by the teacher’s own grading decision. This comparison makes it possible to ask whether Black and White students who appear comparable in externally measured mathematics achievement nevertheless receive different teacher-assigned grades. The paper also connects this question to models of statistical discrimination. In the logic of Altonji and Pierret (2001), decision-makers may initially rely partly on easily observable group characteristics when individual-specific information is limited, but the role of such group information should change as more individual information becomes available. 

Against this background, the central empirical question can be stated precisely:

> *Do Black students receive lower teacher-assigned mathematics grades than comparable White classmates in São Paulo public schools, conditional on blindly scored mathematics performance and observed background characteristics?*

Even conditional comparisons require caution because standardized test scores may measure proficiency with error, and teachers may observe relevant aspects of student performance that are not fully available to the econometrician. For that reason, the analysis develops step by step and interprets the results conservatively.

The next exercise introduces the core variables and the descriptive structure of the dataset.

## Exercise 2 -- Descriptive structure of the data

This exercise begins the descriptive analysis.

At this stage, we document the structure of the variables and the sample on which later conditional comparisons will be based. The analysis in the later exercises will primarily build on a small number of key variables. For that reason, it is important to understand these variables clearly before moving on.

### 2.1 Load the data

In this task, you load the dataset and the packages needed for the first descriptive steps. The object data will be used to inspect the structure of the working sample.

Load the data and the packages used in this exercise.

```{r "2_1"}
library(haven)
library(dplyr)

data <- read_dta("racial_discrimination_grading_AEJ.dta")
```

The first step in any empirical analysis is to understand what one row of the dataset represents.

In this dataset, each row corresponds to one student. The variables in a row therefore describe the same individual student: their school, classroom, teacher-assigned grade, blindly scored test score, and further background information.

Here, you select the identifiers, the teacher-assigned mathematics grade, the two blindly scored test variables, and the two race indicators used for the first Black-White comparison.

Display a small set of key variables for the first observations.

```{r "2_2"}
data |>
  select(
    student_id,
    school_id,
    fe_class,
    ___,
    zscore_mat2010,
    zscore_lp2010,
    rstd_white,
    ___
  ) |>
  slice(1:6)
```

The variables shown here already contain the core empirical ingredients of the problem set.

`student_id` identifies the student, `school_id` identifies the school, and `fe_class` identifies the classroom. The variable `zmathg_2010` records the teacher-assigned mathematics grade in z-standardized form. The variable `zscore_mat2010` records the blindly scored standardized mathematics test score, while `zscore_lp2010` records the blindly scored standardized reading test score. What z-standardization means in this context is explained below.

A crucial feature of these proficiency-test scores is that they are externally and blindly scored. Botelho et al. (sec. I, fn. 5) explicitly state that "Individual-level test results, past or current, are *never* made available to children, parents, teachers, or school principals." The scores could therefore not directly inform teachers' final classroom assessments and provide an external measure of student proficiency.

Finally, `rstd_white` and `rstd_black` are indicator variables equal to one for White or Black students, respectively. The displayed excerpt omits the additional race indicators `rstd_brown` and `rstd_othrace` used in the full dataset. This is why some students in the preview are coded as neither White nor Black in the two columns shown here.

At this point, the most important substantive distinction is the following: `zmathg_2010` is the teacher-assigned mathematics grade in class, whereas `zscore_mat2010` and `zscore_lp2010` are externally scored achievement measures.

### 2.2 The size of the empirical setting

Before turning to group differences or regression results, it is useful to describe the size of the working dataset. The number of observations matters for the empirical analysis, but it should not be overinterpreted. A large dataset can provide a more precise empirical description than a small classroom sample. However, sample size alone does not solve the main identification problems of the paper. The data contain not only many students, but also many classrooms and schools.

Compute the number of students, classrooms, and schools in the working dataset.

```{r "2_3"}
data |>
  summarise(
    n_students = ___,
    n_classes = n_distinct(___),
    n_schools = n_distinct(___)
  )
```

The working dataset contains 277,444 students, 10,614 classrooms, and 3,511 schools. Following the authors, this can be described as a uniquely detailed and large administrative dataset rather than a small classroom sample. It gives the analysis a broad empirical base and allows later within-classroom comparisons to be made across a large number of classroom settings. 

The working dataset is not the universe of all eighth-grade students. It is the restricted analysis sample used by the authors. The restrictions require sufficient availability of transcripts and current and past test scores within the classroom, racially nonhomogeneous classrooms with at least one Black and one White student, and at least 15 students per classroom (Botelho et al., 2015, sec. I).

The next step is to understand the scale of the core variables. The output above tells us how many observations, classrooms, and schools are available. But to interpret means, gaps, and later regression coefficients, we also need to know what the numerical values of the main grade and test-score variables mean. This is why we next turn to z-standardization.

### 2.3 Z-standardization

Before looking at variable means, it is useful to understand the scale of the core performance variables used throughout the analysis.

The three central performance variables are:

* `zmathg_2010`, the teacher-assigned mathematics grade,
* `zscore_mat2010`, the blindly scored mathematics test,
* `zscore_lp2010`, the blindly scored reading test.

All three variables are expressed in *z-standardized form*. A z-standardized value, or z-score, expresses how far an observation lies from the mean of the underlying variable in standard deviation units. This is obtained by subtracting the mean of the variable and dividing the result by its standard deviation, following the standard definition of a z-score, see Illowsky and Dean (2023, ch. 6.1). Formally, for a variable $x$, the standardized value $z$ is given by:

$$z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{sd(x)}$$

This transformation changes the unit of measurement. After standardization, the variable is no longer measured in its original raw units, but in standard deviation units relative to its mean. A value of 0 implies that an observation lies at the mean of the underlying variable.

As the authors state, according to official guidelines, teacher-assigned grades in São Paulo are numeric integer grades ranging from 0 to 10, with a passing grade set at 5 points for all disciplines (Botelho et al., 2015, sec. I). Standardization places the grade and test-score variables on a common scale and makes later differences easier to interpret. For a general discussion of scaling regression inputs, see Gelman (2008, pp. 2865–2866). In particular, once a variable is standardized, a group difference can be read in standard deviation units. For example, if a later estimated grade gap is -0.1, this means that the average teacher-assigned grade of one group is lower by 0.1 standard deviations relative to the comparison group, conditional on the specification being estimated.

Z-standardization therefore helps express differences on a common and interpretable scale. However, the role of standardization is limited. It does not by itself solve any identification problem. It gives the central performance variables a common scale so that descriptive differences and later regression coefficients can be interpreted more clearly.

### 2.4 The average level of the core performance variables

With that scaling in mind, we can now look at the average level of the three central performance variables in the data.


Quiz: What should we expect for the mean of the standardized teacher grade in the working dataset? Take a guess!

(1) around 0
(2) around 1
(3) around 5
(4) around 10

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run line to answer the quiz above
answer.quiz("ex2_quiz_1")
```

Compute the mean of the teacher-assigned mathematics grade `zmathg_2010`, the blind mathematics test score `zscore_mat2010`, and the blind reading test score `zscore_lp2010`.

```{r "2_4"}
data |>
  summarise(
    mean_math_grade = round(mean(___, na.rm = TRUE), 5),
    mean_math_score = round(mean(___, na.rm = TRUE), 5),
    mean_reading_score = round(mean(___, na.rm = TRUE), 5)
  )
```


You should obtain values close to the following:

* $mean\_math\_grade$ = -0.01050
* $mean\_math\_score$ = 0.22150
* $mean\_reading\_score$ = 0.00064

These numbers are mainly useful for orientation. Because the variables are z-standardized, their values are measured in standard-deviation units relative to the reference distribution used for standardization. In the restricted working sample used here, the means do not have to be exactly zero. The positive mean of the blind mathematics score illustrates this point. 

At the moment, the important lesson is not the exact magnitude of these means, but the distinction between the variables themselves: one reflects teacher evaluation, the other two reflect externally scored achievement.

### 2.5 Group composition in the sample

The next descriptive step is to examine the racial composition of the sample.

The race variables used in the analysis are mutually exclusive binary indicators. For student race, `rstd_black` refers to Black students only, while Brown students are coded separately as `rstd_brown`. Thus, the Black-White comparison in the paper is not a broader nonwhite-White comparison. Brown and Other students are separate categories and are either shown separately in descriptive statistics or controlled for separately in the regression specifications. Each variable equals 1 if the student belongs to the respective racial group and 0 otherwise. Their means therefore correspond to the sample shares of the respective groups.

Compute the sample shares of White, Black, Brown, and Other students.

```{r "2_5"}
data |>
  summarise(
    white = round(mean(rstd_white, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    black = round(mean(___, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    brown = round(mean(___, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    other = round(mean(rstd_othrace, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
  )
```

You should obtain values close to:

* $white$ = 0.445
* $black$ = 0.102
* $brown$ = 0.395
* $other$ = 0.059

The sample is therefore not evenly split across racial groups. White and Brown students account for most observations, while Black students account
for about 10 percent. This imbalance should be kept in mind when
interpreting precision. All else equal, larger groups tend to allow more precise estimates and greater statistical power than smaller groups (Faul et al., 2007; Lakens, 2022). However, the Black group still contains many thousands of observations, so the later estimates should be judged primarily from coefficients and clustered standard errors, not from group shares alone.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run for additional info in the Viewer pane
info("Statistical background")
```

However, these group shares do not in themselves provide evidence on grading differences, especially because the analysis is restricted to nonhomogeneous classrooms with at least one Black and one White student and at least 15 students per classroom (Botelho et al., 2015, sec. I). They describe only the composition of the estimation sample, not the source of any subsequent grading gap.

Exercise 2 has established the descriptive foundation of the analysis. We now know what one observation represents, how many students, classrooms, and schools are included in the working dataset, which variables are central, and how the main performance variables are scaled.

The next step is to look at the first visible empirical pattern in the data. We will therefore move from variable understanding to graphical and numerical descriptive evidence on teacher-assigned grades and blindly scored mathematics test performance.

## Exercise 3 -- Descriptive evidence

This exercise introduces the first empirical pattern in the data.

We do not estimate a causal discrimination effect here. At this stage, the goal is descriptive: to examine how teacher-assigned mathematics grades and blindly scored mathematics test score are related for White and Black students and to quantify the raw Black-White grade gaps. 

### 3.1 Preparing the descriptive graph

We begin with a smoothed graph of teacher-assigned mathematics grades against blindly scored mathematics test score.


For the graph in this problem set, we constrain the data to observations where the teacher responded to the questionnaire, using observations with `trespondingQ` equal to 1. In practice, the graph is therefore drawn for the subsample of classrooms in which teacher-side survey information is available. Within this subsample, we also restrict the plotted standardized mathematics score to values strictly between -3 and 3. This removes extreme tails from the display and prevents a very small number of observations from dominating the visual appearance of the figure.

Load the data and the packages used in this section. Afterwards prepare the graph sample.

```{r "3_1"}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

data <- read_dta("racial_discrimination_grading_AEJ.dta")
```

After loading the data, we now construct the plotting sample. This chunk keeps only observations with responding teachers and restricts the displayed mathematics-score range to values between -3 and 3 to avoid extreme tails in the graph.

```{r "3_2"}
fig1_data <- data |>
  filter(___ == 1) |>
  mutate(z_math_graph = ___) |>
  filter(z_math_graph > ___, z_math_graph < ___)
```

### 3.2 Smoothed grade-performance curves

A raw scatter plot can be uninformative in a dataset of this size. For that reason, we use *Locally Weighted Scatterplot Smoothing* (LOWESS smoothing). It simply summarizes the broad relationship between the two variables in a visually readable way (Cleveland, W. S., 1979). The smoothing parameter is set to `f` = 0.8, which is used here to approximate the smoothing choice behind the original figure in the paper.

Generate the data frames for the smoothed curves for White and Black students and combine them in one data frame. Start with the data for the White students.

```{r "3_3"}
white_lowess <- fig1_data |>
  filter(___ == 1) |>
  with(
    lowess(
      x = z_math_graph,
      y = ___,
      f = 0.8
    )
  )
```

Continue with the data for the Black students.

```{r "3_4"}
black_lowess <- fig1_data |>
  filter(___ == 1) |>
  with(
    lowess(
      x = z_math_graph,
      y = ___,
      f = 0.8
    )
  )
```

The two LOWESS objects are lists containing x- and y-values. In the next step, we convert both curves into data frames and stack them into one plotting data frame.

```{r "3_5"}
plot_df <- ___(
  data.frame(
    z_math_graph = white_lowess$x,
    teacher_grade = white_lowess$y,
    group = "___"
  ),
  data.frame(
    z_math_graph = black_lowess$x,
    teacher_grade = black_lowess$y,
    group = "___"
  )
)
```

The plotting code uses the combined data frame from the previous step. The graph relates two variables directly. The horizontal axis shows blindly scored mathematics test performance, and the vertical axis shows the teacher-assigned mathematics grade. The line type separates White and Black students.

If the teacher-assigned grade moved in exactly the same way with observed mathematics performance for both groups, then the two curves would lie very close together.

Plot the two smoothed curves.

```{r "3_6"}
ggplot(
  plot_df,
  aes(
    x = ___,
    y = ___,
    color = group,
    linetype = group
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "White" = "lightgrey",
      "Black" = "black"
    )
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "White" = "solid",
      "Black" = "dashed"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Blindly-scored math test, 2010 (z-score)",
    y = "Teacher-assigned math grade, 2010 (z-score)",
    color = NULL,
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


The graph contains two descriptive facts.

First, both curves slope upward. Students with higher blind mathematics scores also tend to receive better teacher-assigned mathematics grades. This positive association is exactly what one would expect and what is consistent with grades responding positively to measured achievement.

Second, the light grey curve, representing the White students, lies above the black dashed curve, representing the Black students, throughout the plotted score range. This indicates that, within the visible range of blindly scored mathematics performance, White students tend to receive higher teacher-assigned mathematics grades than Black students at similar observed mathematics test-score levels.

This descriptive pattern motivates the controlled comparisons in the next exercise. The graph shows that teacher-assigned grades and blindly scored test performance do not line up in exactly the same way across the two groups. It does not show why this difference appears, and it does not yet control for other observed or unobserved student characteristics.


Quiz: Why is the smoothed grade-performance graph not enough to identify differential grading?

(1) It does not control for other observed or unobserved student characteristics.
(2) It uses too many observations.
(3) It compares only standardized variables.
(4) It includes White students as the omitted group.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run line to answer the quiz above
answer.quiz("ex3_quiz_descriptive")
```

### 3.3 Descriptive means by race

The graph is useful, but it is not enough on its own. We now complement it with a compact descriptive table. The graph above follows the restricted sample used for the descriptive figure. For the following mean comparisons, we return to the full working sample unless stated otherwise.

The purpose of the following table is to check whether the raw grade difference appears alone or together with broader differences in achievement. For that reason, we compare White and Black students in the three central variables mentioned earlier:

* `zmathg_2010`: standardized, current teacher-assigned mathematics grade (2010),
* `zscore_mat2010`: standardized, current blind mathematics test score (2010),
* `pastMATgrade`: standardized, earlier mathematics grade (2009).

The third variable matters because it adds a measure of prior school performance. This helps us see whether the current grade gap is part of a broader pattern of performance differences over time.

Compute group means for White and Black students.

```{r "3_7"}
data |>
  filter(rstd_white == 1 | rstd_black == 1) |>
  mutate(race = ifelse(___ == 1, "White", "Black")) |>
  group_by(race) |>
  summarise(
    teacher_grade = round(mean(zmathg_2010, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    blind_math_score = round(mean(zscore_mat2010, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    past_math_grade = round(mean(pastMATgrade, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
  )
```

This table should show the same pattern in all three variables: Black students have lower average current teacher-assigned mathematics grades, lower average current blindly scored mathematics test score, and lower average earlier mathematics grades.


Quiz: Why is the raw grade gap not enough to show differential grading?

(1) It appears together with differences in test scores and past grades.
(2) It is based on too few observations.
(3) It uses a non-standard outcome scale.
(4) It is indeed enough to show differential grading.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run line to answer the quiz above
answer.quiz("ex3_quiz_means")
```

The raw grade difference is therefore not an isolated fact that appears only in current teacher-assigned grades. It appears together with differences in current externally measured mathematics performance and in earlier mathematics performance.

This is already informative. It suggests that the raw grade gap is closely associated with broader observed achievement differences and not only with current grading decisions.

### 3.4 Raw Black-White differences

To make the descriptive comparison sharper, we now compute the Black-minus-White difference directly for the same three variables.

Write the function `gap_mean`, which conducts the raw Black-minus-White differences.

```{r "3_8"}
gap_mean <- function(var) {
  mean(var[data$rstd_black == 1], na.rm = TRUE) -
    mean(var[data$___ == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

Now, compute the raw Black-minus-White differences using the function `gap_mean`.

```{r "3_9"}
raw_gaps <- tibble(
  variable = c(
    "teacher_grade",
    "blind_math_score",
    "past_math_grade"
  ),
  black_minus_white = c(
    gap_mean(data$___),
    gap_mean(data$___),
    gap_mean(data$___)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    black_minus_white = signif(black_minus_white, 3)
  )
```

Display the raw Black-White differences in the key performance variables.

```{r "3_10"}
kable(
  raw_gaps,
  caption = "Raw Black-White differences in key performance variables"
)
```

You should obtain a raw Black-White gap in current teacher-assigned mathematics grades close to -0.338.

That number has a precise interpretation. Because `zmathg_2010` is standardized, a value of -0.338 means that the average teacher-assigned mathematics grade of a Black student is lower by about 0.338 standard deviations than that of an average White student.

But the rest of the table matters just as much. The current blind mathematics score difference is also negative with a value of -0.354, and the earlier mathematics-grade difference with a value of -0.346 as well. So, the current grade gap appears together with lower current blindly scored mathematics test performance and lower earlier mathematics performance.

The results show that the raw grade gap is embedded in a broader pattern of observed achievement differences. The raw difference in current teacher-assigned grades therefore cannot be interpreted as a clean estimate of differential grading or racial discrimination. Part of the raw difference may be associated with differences that are already visible in external test performance and earlier school achievement.

### 3.5 What the descriptive evidence shows

The descriptive evidence shows a clear starting point for the regression analysis.

First, teacher-assigned mathematics grades are positively associated with blindly scored mathematics performance for both White and Black students. 

Second, the smoothed grade-performance curves differ by race. Over the plotted score range shown here, White students tend to receive higher teacher-assigned mathematics grades than Black students with similar blindly scored mathematics performance. 

Third, the raw Black-White gap in current teacher-assigned mathematics grades is substantial, about -0.338 standard deviations. However, this raw grade gap appears together with negative Black-White differences in current blindly scored mathematics performance and earlier mathematics grades.

This pattern is important because the raw grade gap cannot be interpreted as a clean estimate of differential grading or racial discrimination. The raw gap seems to be mixed together with broader achievement differences that are already visible in the data.

The next exercise therefore moves from raw descriptive evidence to regression-based comparisons and studies how the coefficient on `rstd_black` changes once additional observed information is introduced step by step.

## Exercise 4 -- Controlled comparisons of teacher-assigned mathematics grades

The previous exercise established a raw Black-White gap of about -0.338 standard deviations in current teacher-assigned mathematics grades. It also showed that this raw grade gap appears together with differences in current blindly scored mathematics test performance and earlier mathematics grades.

The next step is to move from raw descriptive comparisons to *controlled comparisons*. The purpose is to examine how much of the raw Black-White grade gap remains once additional observed information is taken into account step by step.

The dependent variable in this exercise remains `zmathg_2010`, the current teacher-assigned mathematics grade in standardized form.

### 4.1 OLS as a controlled comparison

The method used here is ordinary least squares (OLS).

More generally, a regression model relates one dependent variable to one or more explanatory variables. In the present setting, the full race-indicator specification can be written as

$$zmathg\_2010_i =
\beta_0 + 
\beta_1 rstd\_black_i + 
\beta_2 rstd\_brown_i + 
\beta_3 rstd\_othrace_i + 
\gamma'X_i + 
u_i.$$

In this equation, $zmathg\_2010_i$ denotes the teacher-assigned mathematics grade of student $i$, measured in z-scores. The variables $rstd\_black_i$, $rstd\_brown_i$, and $rstd\_othrace_i$ are race indicators. White students form the omitted reference group. The vector $X_i$ collects further observed control variables, such as current test scores, child demographic characteristics, past grades, or family-background measures. The error term $u_i$ contains all remaining determinants of the outcome that are not explicitly included in the regression.

For readability, the following mathematical expressions display only the Black indicator explicitly. This is only a notational simplification. In the actual regressions, the Brown and Other race indicators are still included, so the coefficient on `rstd_black` is interpreted relative to the omitted White reference group.

The coefficient $\beta_1$ is of central interest here. Since `rstd_black` is a binary indicator, $\beta_1$ measures the difference in the predicted teacher-assigned math grade between Black students and otherwise comparable White students, where comparability depends on the controls included in $X_i$.

Using the simplified notation, OLS estimates the coefficients by choosing the values of $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, and $\gamma$ that minimize the sum of squared residuals.

A residual is the gap between the observed outcome and the value predicted by the regression model for a given observation. By squaring and summing these residuals across all students, OLS gives more weight to larger prediction errors and selects the coefficient values that make the fitted regression line come as close as possible to the observed data overall. For the OLS interpretation used here, see Wooldridge (2010, ch. 3).

In this exercise, OLS is not introduced because it is automatically causal. It is introduced because it provides a systematic way to compare students conditionally on observed information. Once additional variables are included in the regression, the coefficient on `rstd_black` is no longer a raw mean difference. It becomes the conditional association between Black student status and current teacher-assigned mathematics grades, given the controls included in that specification.

### 4.2 Classroom fixed effects

The fixed-effects logic follows Wooldridge’s unobserved-effects framework: fixed effects allow unobserved group-level heterogeneity to be correlated with observed covariates and can be implemented through group indicators. In the present application, the group is the classroom. Classroom fixed effects therefore absorb classroom-level differences shared by classmates, while the race coefficients are estimated from variation between students within the same classroom (Wooldridge, 2010, ch. 10).

This is necessary even though the underlying sample is already restricted to racially mixed classrooms with at least one Black and one White student and at least 15 students. The replication dataset used here already corresponds to the paper's working sample after the relevant classroom restrictions. These restrictions make within-classroom Black-White comparisons possible, but they do not by themselves remove differences in grading environments across classrooms.

To see why classroom fixed effects are still needed, consider two classrooms. One classroom may have a generally strict teacher who gives relatively low grades to all students. Another classroom may have a more lenient teacher who grades all students more generously. If Black and White students are unevenly distributed across such classrooms, then part of the raw grade gap could reflect differences in classroom-level grading environments rather than differences between students within the same classroom.

Classroom fixed effects address this problem by absorbing all factors that are common to students in the same classroom $c$. This includes the teacher's general grading level, classroom-wide grading standards, the classroom environment, and other shared classroom-level features. They do not remove student-level differences within classrooms.

With classroom fixed effects, the simplified model can be written as

$$zmathg\_2010_{ic} =
\beta_1 rstd\_black_{ic} +
\gamma'X_{ic} +
\alpha_c +
u_{ic}.$$

Here, the term $\alpha_c$ is a classroom fixed effect. It absorbs all factors that are common to students in classroom $c$, such as the teacher's general grading level, classroom-wide grading standards, and other shared classroom-level conditions.

After classroom fixed effects are introduced, the coefficient on `rstd_black` is identified from differences between students *within the same classroom*. This removes classroom-level confounding common to all students in a classroom, but it does not remove student-level differences within classrooms. Classroom fixed effects are therefore an important step in the empirical strategy, not a complete identification solution.


Quiz: What do classroom fixed effects absorb in this setting?

(1) Factors common to all students in the same classroom.
(2) All student-level differences within a classroom.
(3) Measurement error in current test scores.
(4) The effect of student race.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run line to answer the quiz above
answer.quiz("ex4_quiz_fe")
```

### 4.3 Raw OLS regression, and first fixed-effects comparison

The raw Black-White grade gap from the previous exercise can also be written as a regression coefficient. To see this, estimate a regression of `zmathg_2010` on the race indicators only. Because White students are the omitted reference group, the coefficient on `rstd_black` measures the difference between Black and White students in current teacher-assigned mathematics grades.

In this simple OLS regression, no additional controls are included. Therefore, the coefficient on `rstd_black` still represents a raw Black-White comparison, not a richly controlled comparison. The advantage of writing the raw gap as a regression is that the same framework can then be extended step by step by adding classroom fixed effects and further observed control variables.

The simple race-indicator regression is

$$zmathg\_2010_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 rstd\_black_i + \beta_2 rstd\_brown_i + \beta_3 rstd\_othrace_i + u_i.$$

Here, the coefficient on `rstd_black` should be close to -0.338, matching the raw Black-White gap from the previous exercise.

Before estimating the full sequence of controlled models, it is useful to inspect the first two steps directly. The first column estimates the raw Black-White gap as an OLS regression with race indicators only. This is the regression version of the descriptive gap from the previous exercise. The second column adds classroom fixed effects to the same race-indicator specification. This shows how the comparison changes once students are compared within the same classroom.

Load the data and required packages.

```{r "4_1"}
library(fixest)
library(lfe)
library(stargazer)

data <- read_dta("racial_discrimination_grading_AEJ.dta")
```

Estimate the raw OLS regression. The first model contains only the race indicators. Since White students are the omitted reference group, the coefficient on `rstd_black` is the regression version of the raw Black-White grade gap.

```{r "4_2"}
ols_example <- felm(
  zmathg_2010 ~ ___ + rstd_brown + rstd_othrace |
    0 | 0 | fe_class,
  data = data
)
```

Estimate the corresponding classroom fixed-effects model. This model uses the same race indicators but adds classroom fixed effects. The coefficient on `rstd_black` is now identified from within-classroom comparisons.

```{r "4_3"}
fe_example <- felm(
  zmathg_2010 ~ rstd_black + rstd_brown + rstd_othrace |
    ___ | 0 | fe_class,
  data = data
)
```

Display the two models in one compact table. Create a nice view of the regressions with `stargazer`.

```{r "4_4"}
stargazer(
  ols_example,
  fe_example,
  type = "text",
  title = "OLS and classroom fixed-effects comparison",
  column.labels = c("Raw OLS", "Class FE"),
  dep.var.labels = "Teacher-assigned math grade",
  covariate.labels = c(
    "Black student",
    "Brown student",
    "Other race"
  ),
  keep = c("rstd_black", "rstd_brown", "rstd_othrace"),
  omit.stat = c("f", "ser"),
  digits = 3,
  notes = paste(
    "Clustered standard errors at classroom level",
    "are reported in parentheses."
  )
)
```

The two columns show the same race indicators under two different comparison standards. The OLS column compares students across the full working sample. In this specification, the coefficient on `rstd_black` should be close to -0.338, which corresponds to the raw Black-White gap from the previous exercise expressed as a regression coefficient.

The classroom fixed-effects column compares students within the same classroom, because classroom-level differences are absorbed by the fixed effects. The coefficient on `rstd_black` becomes smaller, but it remains negative (-0.296). This means that part of the raw gap is associated with differences across classrooms, but a substantial negative difference remains even within classrooms.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run for additional info in the Viewer pane
info("felm() from lfe")
```

This explicit regression table is shown only once to make the mechanics of the estimation transparent. In the remaining part of the exercise, the model sequence becomes richer and includes score polynomials, child demographics, past grades, and family-background variables. Showing all coefficients from all specifications would make the output unnecessarily crowded. Therefore, the next steps keep the full models in the background and extract only the coefficient on `rstd_black`, its standard error, its p-value, and the change in its absolute value across specifications.

### 4.4 Variable blocks used in the controlled comparisons

The regression sequence introduces observed information in blocks. This is useful because the blocks correspond to different types of characteristics that may be related both to teacher-assigned mathematics grades and to the raw Black-White grade gap.

In this exercise, we focus on observed test performance, child demographics, past mathematics grades, and family background. Variables more directly related to classroom behavior, effort, and teacher-observed student traits are introduced in the next exercise.

Define the variable blocks used in the model sequence.

```{r "4_5"}
# These variable blocks are used in the model sequence below.
# They are defined once here to avoid repeating long formulas.
scores <- c(
  "zscore_mat2010", "zscore_mat2010_sq", "zscore_mat2010_3",
  "zscore_mat2010_4", "interzscore_mat2010",
  "interzscore_mat2010_sq", "interzscore_mat2010_3",
  "interzscore_mat2010_4", "zscore_lp2010"
)

child_demog <- c(
  "mstd_boy",
  "rstd_age",
  "rstd_age_sq"
)

past_grades <- c(
  "pastMATgrade"
)

parent_ses_demog <- c(
  "I_noparQUEST", "pq_momnoschool", "pq_momchs",
  "pq_momincoll", "pq_momccoll", "pq_DKmomschool",
  "pq_momage16to24", "pq_momage25to34", "pq_momage45to59",
  "pq_momage60up", "pq_DKmomage", "pq_mombornSPs",
  "pq_mombornabroad", "pq_DKmomborn", "pq_homeown",
  "pq_DKhomeown", "nr_autos", "Inr_autos", "nr_wcs", "Inr_wcs"
)
```

These blocks have distinct roles.


Quiz: In which block does nr_autos belong? Take a guess!

(1) scores
(2) past_grades
(3) parent_ses_demog
(4) child_demog

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run line to answer the quiz above
answer.quiz("ex4_quiz_1")
```


Quiz: Why is pastMATgrade introduced after the current-score control block? Take a guess!

(1) Because earlier mathematics grades may contain additional longer-run performance information not fully captured by the current blind score.
(2) Because earlier grades are always causally cleaner than current scores.
(3) Because fixed effects require lagged dependent variables.
(4) Because family background can only be added after past grades.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run line to answer the quiz above
answer.quiz("ex4_quiz_2")
```

The `scores` block contains current blindly scored mathematics test performance, current blind reading performance, and a flexible functional form of these score measures. Following the paper, current mathematics performance enters as a fourth-order polynomial, reading performance enters linearly, and the variables beginning with `interzscore_` capture interactions between current reading proficiency and powers of current mathematics proficiency. These interaction terms allow the relationship between teacher-assigned mathematics grades and blindly scored mathematics test performance to vary with reading proficiency. They are not race interactions. The block is therefore meant to control flexibly for observed academic achievement, rather than only for a single linear mathematics-score difference.

The `child_demog` block contains basic demographic characteristics: gender, age, and age squared. These variables are not the main focus of the study, but they may still be associated with grading, performance, or classroom placement. Including them makes the comparison more demanding by holding constant basic observed demographic differences between students.

The `past_grades` block contains `pastMATgrade`, an earlier teacher-assigned mathematics grade. This variable is useful because current blind test performance may not fully summarize longer-run school performance. Earlier mathematics grades may contain persistent achievement information that still matters for current teacher-assigned grades. However, `pastMATgrade` is not a purely neutral control. It is itself a teacher-assigned grade from an earlier period. If earlier teacher judgments were affected by biased assessment, then conditioning on `pastMATgrade` may absorb part of the cumulative effect of earlier discrimination. The paper explicitly recognizes this type of concern and treats the fully controlled specification as conservative.

The `parent_ses_demog` block contains family background and household information, such as maternal education, maternal age, home ownership, number of cars, and number of bathrooms. These variables are included because educational outcomes are often associated with household resources and family circumstances. In this exercise, they are used as part of a richer observed-information set, not as clean causal mediators.

Overall, the sequence should not be interpreted as a causal decomposition of the raw Black-White grade gap. Adding correlated controls is order-sensitive and does not show how much of the gap is caused by a specific block. Instead, the sequence asks whether a coefficient on `rstd_black` remains after progressively controlling for observed achievement, basic demographics, earlier grades, and family background.

### 4.5 The controlled OLS sequence

We now estimate five models.

* **M1**: raw comparison with race indicators only  
* **M2**: M1 plus classroom fixed effects  
* **M3**: M2 plus current observed performance and child demographics  
* **M4**: M3 plus earlier mathematics grade  
* **M5**: M4 plus family background  

This sequence stays close to the OLS progression in the paper while keeping the presentation compact. The purpose is not to claim that each block cleanly explains a separate causal part of the raw gap. The careful interpretation is: the sequence shows how the coefficient on `rstd_black` changes once richer observed information is introduced step by step.

We now estimate the model sequence step by step. The first model is the raw
race-indicator regression.

```{r "4_6"}
m1 <- feols(
  zmathg_2010 ~ rstd_black + rstd_brown + rstd_othrace,
  data = data,
  vcov = ~___
)
```

The second model adds classroom fixed effects.

```{r "4_7"}
m2 <- feols(
  zmathg_2010 ~ rstd_black + rstd_brown + rstd_othrace |
    ___,
  data = data,
  vcov = ~fe_class
)
```

Before estimating the remaining models, we define which control blocks enter each specification. M3 adds current-score controls and child demographics.

```{r "4_8"}
controls_m3 <- c(scores, ___)
```

M4 keeps the M3 controls and adds the earlier mathematics grade.

```{r "4_9"}
controls_m4 <- c(scores, child_demog, ___)
```

M5 is the richest OLS specification in this exercise. It adds family background to the previous controls.

```{r "4_10"}
controls_m5 <- c(scores, child_demog, past_grades, ___)
```

M3 adds current-score controls and child demographics to the
within-classroom comparison.

```{r "4_11"}
m3 <- feols(
  as.formula(
    paste(
      "zmathg_2010 ~ rstd_black + rstd_brown +",
      "rstd_othrace +",
      paste(___, collapse = " + "),
      "| fe_class"
    )
  ),
  data = data,
  vcov = ~___
)
```

M4 keeps the M3 controls and adds the earlier teacher-assigned mathematics grade.

```{r "4_12"}
m4 <- feols(
  as.formula(
    paste(
      "zmathg_2010 ~ rstd_black + rstd_brown +",
      "rstd_othrace +",
      paste(___, collapse = " + "),
      "| fe_class"
    )
  ),
  data = data,
  vcov = ~___
)
```

M5 adds family-background controls and is the richest OLS specification in this exercise.

```{r "4_13"}
m5 <- feols(
  as.formula(
    paste(
      "zmathg_2010 ~ rstd_black + rstd_brown +",
      "rstd_othrace +",
      paste(___, collapse = " + "),
      "| fe_class"
    )
  ),
  data = data,
  vcov = ~___
)
```

Each of these models asks about the same dependent variable, but under a different comparison standard. The later models do not merely add variables. They change the comparison by holding increasingly rich observed information constant.

The clearest summary of the regression sequence is the path of the coefficient on `rstd_black`. The previous table showed one OLS model and one fixed-effects model explicitly. We now apply the same logic to the full sequence of specifications, but report only the coefficient on `rstd_black`, its standard error, the p-value, the significance level, and the change in absolute value relative to the previous model.

We first collect the five estimated models in a list. This makes it possible to extract the same coefficient from all models with the same code.

```{r "4_14"}
models_ols <- list(___, ___, ___, ___, ___)
```

Next, extract the coefficient on `rstd_black` from each model.

```{r "4_15"}
black_coef <- sapply(
  models_ols,
  function(m) coef(m)[___]
)
```

Finally, extract the corresponding clustered standard errors.

```{r "4_16"}
black_se <- sapply(
  models_ols,
  function(m) se(m)[___]
)
```

The p-value tests whether the estimated coefficient for Black students differs statistically from zero. In this table, the null hypothesis is that the coefficient on the Black indicator equals zero, meaning that there is no estimated difference in teacher-assigned math grades between Black and White students within the respective model specification.

Technically, the p-value gives the probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained, assuming that the null hypothesis and the statistical model are correct. A small p-value therefore indicates that the estimated coefficient is difficult to reconcile with the null hypothesis. However, the p-value does not measure the size or practical importance of the effect, and it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

```{r "4_17"}
black_tstat <- black_coef / black_se

p_value_t <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(black_tstat))

p_value <- ifelse(
  p_value_t < 0.01,
  "<0.01",
  as.character(round(p_value_t, 4))
)
```

The following chunk collects the extracted coefficients in a compact table.

```{r "4_18"}
coef_path_ols <- tibble(
  Model = c(
    "M1: raw comparison",
    "M2: + classroom fixed effects",
    "M3: + scores and child demographics",
    "M4: + past math grade",
    "M5: + family background"
  ),
  `Black coef. (SE)` = paste0(round(black_coef, 3), " (", round(black_se,3), ")"),
  p = p_value,
  Change = round(
    c(NA, diff(abs(black_coef)) * -1),
    3
  )
)

kable(coef_path_ols, digits = 3,
        caption = "Path of the Black coefficient across OLS specifications"
)
```


You should obtain coefficients close to the following:

* **M1**: -0.338
* **M2**: -0.296
* **M3**: -0.094
* **M4**: -0.045
* **M5**: -0.043

The changes in absolute value are approximately:

* **M1** to **M2**: 0.042
* **M2** to **M3**: 0.202
* **M3** to **M4**: 0.049
* **M4** to **M5**: 0.002

A positive value in Change means that the absolute size of the Black coefficient decreases relative to the previous specification.

The p-values are reported as < 0.01 whenever they are smaller than 0.01. This avoids the misleading impression that very small p-values are exactly zero.

The movement of the coefficient on `rstd_black` should be interpreted carefully. It is not a causal decomposition of the raw Black-White grade gap. Sequentially adding correlated control blocks is order-sensitive and does not identify how much each block independently explains the gap, see Gelbach (2016). Botelho et al. (2015, sec. III) make the same caution when presenting their OLS sequence. The sequence is nevertheless informative because it shows how sensitive the residual Black-White grade gap is to increasingly rich conditioning sets.

In **M1**, the coefficient is about -0.338. This is the raw Black-White grade gap expressed in regression form. In **M2**, the coefficient becomes about -0.296, which means that the gap becomes somewhat smaller once classroom-level common factors are absorbed, but a substantial negative within-classroom difference remains.

In **M3**, the coefficient moves sharply toward zero, to about -0.094. This is the largest movement in the sequence and shows that the coefficient on `rstd_black` is highly sensitive to conditioning on current observed performance and child demographics.

In **M4**, the coefficient becomes about -0.045. Earlier mathematics grades therefore appear to contain additional performance-related information associated with current teacher evaluations. However, `pastMATgrade` is itself teacher-assigned and may partly reflect earlier assessment practices. It should therefore not be interpreted as a purely objective control.

In **M5**, the coefficient changes only slightly, from about -0.045 to about -0.043. Adding family background is therefore associated with very little additional movement once current scores, child demographics, and earlier mathematics grades are already included.

### 4.6 What this exercise has established

This exercise has moved the analysis from raw descriptive comparisons to controlled regression-based comparisons. The raw Black-White gap in teacher-assigned mathematics grades becomes progressively smaller once richer observed information is taken into account. The largest reduction occurs when current observed performance and child demographics enter the model. In the richest specification of this exercise, however, a small negative residual coefficient of about -0.043 remains.

Two distinct interpretation issues remain. The first is *unobserved heterogeneity*: teachers may observe productive student traits, such as effort or classroom conduct, that are only imperfectly observed in the data. The second is *measurement error*: the current blind test-score block may be a noisy measure of the underlying proficiency that teachers try to assess.

The next exercise focuses on the first concern by adding proxy controls for teacher-observed productive traits. The following exercise then turns to measurement error and the fixed-effects instrumental-variables strategy.

## Exercise 5 -- Unobserved heterogeneity and the proxy strategy

The previous exercise controlled for several important observed characteristics. But even within the same classroom and after conditioning on current scores, past grades, and family background, students may still differ in traits that teachers observe more directly than the econometrician.

*Unobserved heterogeneity* means that some grade-relevant student traits are not fully observed in the dataset. In this context, this mainly refers to behavioral and motivational traits that teachers may observe during regular classroom interactions. If such traits affect teacher-assigned grades and are correlated with race, then the remaining coefficient on `rstd_black` could partly reflect omitted productive traits rather than biased grading.

This is one of the main interpretation problems in the paper. Botelho et al. (2015, sec. II) explicitly worry that teachers may observe competencies not captured by proficiency tests, especially behavioral indicators available during classroom interactions. Their response is to include a rich set of proxy controls and examine how sensitive the coefficient on `rstd_black` is to these additional controls.

This exercise examines how the coefficient on `rstd_black` changes when earlier-performance and behavioral proxy variables are added. 

### 5.1 Omitted student-level traits as an identification problem

Consider a simplified grading equation:

$$G_i =
\beta_0 +
\delta black_{i} +
\beta S_i +
\gamma W_i' +
\rho A_i +
\varepsilon_i.$$

Here, $G_i$ is the teacher-assigned mathematics grade. $S_i$ is observed current academic performance. $W_i$ contains other observed controls, such as demographics, past grades, and family background. The variable $A_i$ denotes a productive student attribute that is relevant for grading and observed by the teacher more directly than by the econometrician. Examples include effort, reliability, classroom conduct, responsiveness to instructions, homework discipline, sustained attention, and participation. The coefficient $\rho$ measures how strongly this attribute is associated with teacher-assigned grades. The coefficient $\delta$ is the conditional Black-White grade difference of interest. The term $\varepsilon_i$ contains remaining unobserved determinants of grades.

Now suppose that $A_i$ is omitted from the regression. The estimated coefficient on $black$ may then be biased. The reason is that the omitted attribute becomes part of the regression error. In the shorter regression without $A_i$, the omitted part is

$$\rho A_i + \varepsilon_i.$$

OLS will estimate the coefficient on $black$ correctly only if $black$ is not systematically related to this omitted part, after conditioning on the included controls. If Black and White students with the same observed performance and background still differ in $A_i$, then the omitted attribute can be incorrectly attributed to the coefficient on $black$.

With controls in the model, this logic should be stated in partial terms. Let $\widetilde{black}_i$ be the residual from regressing $black_i$ on the included controls $S_i$ and $W_i$. Intuitively, $\widetilde{black}_i$ is the remaining variation in $black$ after removing the part that is predictable from observed performance and background controls. Similarly, let $\widetilde{A}_i$ be the residual from regressing $A_i$ on the same controls. Logically, $\widetilde{A}_i$ is the part of the productive attribute that is not already captured by the included controls.

The omitted-variable bias in the coefficient on $black$ can then be written as

$$Bias(\hat\delta)
=
\rho
\frac{Cov(\widetilde{black}_i,\widetilde{A}_i)}
{Var(\widetilde{black}_i)}.$$

The sign and size of the bias depend on two parts.

First, $\rho$ tells us whether the omitted attribute affects grades. If productive behavior raises grades, then $\rho > 0$.

Second, the covariance term tells us whether the omitted attribute is still related to $black$ after the observed controls have been removed. If, among students with similar observed scores and background characteristics, Black students have lower values of the omitted productive attribute, then

$$Cov(\widetilde{black}_i,\widetilde{A}_i) < 0.$$

In that case, the bias is negative:

$$\rho > 0
\quad \text{and} \quad
Cov(\widetilde{black}_i,\widetilde{A}_i) < 0
\quad \Rightarrow \quad
Bias(\hat\delta) < 0.$$

The coefficient is biased when the residualized race indicator is correlated with the residualized omitted trait. This expression follows the standard omitted-variable-bias logic for linear regression (Wooldridge, 2010, ch. 3). The residualized notation uses the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem: after partialling out the included controls, the relevant association is the association between the residualized regressor and the residualized omitted variable (Frisch & Waugh, 1933; Lovell, 1963; Lovell, 2008). Interpreting this concern as a sensitivity problem for unobserved confounding follows the same OVB logic emphasized by Cinelli and Hazlett (2020). This means that the estimated Black coefficient would be too negative. The regression would partly attribute lower grades to $black$, although part of the difference would actually come from the omitted productive attribute.

This is the central omitted-heterogeneity concern. A residual Black-White grade gap should therefore not be interpreted as biased grading unless the possibility of omitted productive traits has been taken seriously. This is why the paper adds proxy variables for earlier performance, behavior, effort, and school engagement.


Quiz: Suppose a teacher-observed productive attribute raises grades and is lower for Black students even after conditioning on observed controls. What happens if this attribute is omitted?

(1) The estimated Black coefficient may become too negative.
(2) The estimated Black coefficient may become too positive.
(3) The estimated Black coefficient must become exactly zero.
(4) Classroom fixed effects automatically remove this student-level problem.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run line to answer the quiz above
answer.quiz("ex5_quiz_1")
```

### 5.2 Proxy variables

A proxy is an observed variable that contains information about a concept that is difficult to observe directly. In this exercise, the difficult-to-observe concept is a productive student attribute that teachers may observe during the school year, but that the econometrician observes only imperfectly.

Suppose the teacher observes a productive attribute $A_i$, but the econometrician does not. The econometrician may instead observe a proxy $P_i$:

$$P_i = \lambda A_i + e_i .$$

Here, $P_i$ is the observed imperfect proxy for the latent productive trait $A_i$. For example, parent-reported effort is not the same as true effort, but it may contain information about effort. Student self-reports of skipping class are not the same as true classroom engagement, but they may contain information about school-related behavior. The parameter $\lambda$ captures how strongly the proxy is related to the underlying trait and $e_i$ is proxy measurement error. 

Proxy controls can reduce omitted-variable concerns only to the extent that they contain information about the omitted productive trait. Because proxies are imperfect, they make the comparison more demanding but do not eliminate unobserved heterogeneity.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run for additional info in the Viewer pane
info("Econometric background")
```

### 5.3 Why some proxies are also conceptually delicate

Proxy controls make the comparison more demanding, but they are not
neutral by construction. Imperfect substitutes like parent reports, student self-reports, teacher-recorded measures, past grades, and earlier-performance indicators may all contain relevant information about teacher-observed productive traits. However, if relevant traits remain unobserved and are correlated with race, the residual Black-White grade gap may still partly reflect omitted student-level characteristics.

Some proxies are also conceptually delicate because they may not be predetermined. For example, `pastMATgrade` may contain persistent achievement information, which makes it useful as a control. At the same time, it is itself a teacher-assigned grade from an earlier period. If earlier teacher judgments were biased, then controlling for `pastMATgrade` may absorb part of the very phenomenon the paper is interested in.

A similar concern applies to behavior, effort, and motivation. These variables may be shaped by earlier classroom experiences, feedback, encouragement, discouragement, or prior grading. If earlier biased treatment affected these traits, then controlling for them may mechanically reduce the estimated racial gap.

The proxy strategy therefore trades off two risks. Excluding these controls leaves the analysis more exposed to omitted productive traits. Including them may over-control for variables partly shaped by earlier school treatment. If some controls are downstream outcomes of earlier discriminatory treatment, a fully controlled specification may therefore underestimate the broader racial gap of interest. A conservative interpretation is that a remaining negative coefficient on `rstd_black` is not easily explained away by the available proxy measures, but the exercise still does not prove that all relevant unobserved heterogeneity has been removed.


Quiz: What is the main limitation of proxy controls?

(1) They may measure the omitted trait only imperfectly.
(2) They remove the need for fixed effects.
(3) They are always randomly assigned.
(4) They instrument student race.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Run line to answer the quiz above
answer.quiz("ex5_quiz_proxy")
```

### 5.4 Simulation: Omitted productive traits and imperfect proxies

We now build a simple simulation to show why omitted productive traits can bias the coefficient on `rstd_black` and how proxies can help without fully solving the problem.

The following simulation is adapted from the proxy-control logic discussed in Kranz (2021). The key point is that a proxy can reduce omitted-variable bias if it is strongly correlated with the omitted trait. However, proxy controls do not by themselves create a credible source of exogenous variation. They can make a controlled comparison more informative, but they do not automatically turn it into a causal design.

The simulation contains:

* a race indicator;
* a current performance measure;
* a productive student trait observed by the teacher;
* an imperfect proxy for that trait;
* and a teacher-assigned grade.

Generate a simple dataset.

```{r "5_1"}
set.seed(123)
n <- 100000
black <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.20)
performance <- -0.35 * black + rnorm(n)
trait_true <- -0.25 * black + rnorm(n)
```

Complete the following code to generate the noisy version of the trait.

```{r "5_2"}
trait_proxy <- ___ + rnorm(n, sd = 0.75)
```

Complete the following code to estimate the oracle model.

```{r "5_3"}
grade <- -0.02 * black +
  0.50 * performance +
  0.25 * ___ +
  rnorm(n)
```

Run the following chunk to deploy a simulation tibble.

```{r "5_4"}
sim_proxy <- tibble(
  grade = grade,
  black = black,
  performance = performance,
  trait_true = trait_true,
  trait_proxy = trait_proxy
)
```

The true grading equation is

$$grade_i = -0.02black_{ic} + 0.50performance_i + 0.25trait\_true_i + error_i.$$

So the true conditional coefficient on $black$ is -0.02. In real data, however, the econometrician does not observe the teacher-observed productive trait $trait\_true_i$ perfectly. The simulation therefore compares three cases.

First, the oracle model includes the true productive trait $trait\_true_i$. This is not feasible in real data, but it provides a benchmark. Second, the omitted-trait model leaves the productive trait out. Third, the proxy model adds only the imperfect proxy $trait\_proxy_i$, which the econometrician observes instead of the true productive trait.

The first model is an oracle model. It controls for the true productive trait, which is usually not observed in real data.

```{r "5_5"}
m_oracle <- feols(
  grade ~ black + performance + ___,
  data = sim_proxy
)
```

The second model omits the productive trait entirely.

```{r "5_6"}
m_omit <- feols(
  grade ~ black + ___,
  data = sim_proxy
)
```

The third model controls for the imperfect proxy instead of the true trait.

```{r "5_7"}
m_proxy <- feols(
  grade ~ black + performance + ___,
  data = sim_proxy
)
```

The models have now been estimated. The next chunk extracts the Black coefficient from each model so that the omitted-variable and proxy-control logic can be compared directly.

```{r "5_8"}
proxy_results <- tibble(
  Model = c(
    "Oracle: add true trait",
    "Omit productive trait",
    "Add imperfect proxy"
  ),
  `Black coef.` = signif(c(
    coef(m_oracle)["black"],
    coef(m_omit)["black"],
    coef(m_proxy)["black"]
  ), 2),
  Trait_slope = signif(c(
    coef(m_oracle)["trait_true"],
    NA,
    coef(m_proxy)["trait_proxy"]
  ), 2)
)
```

Now show the simulation results.

```{r "5_9"}
kable(
  proxy_results, digits = 3,
  caption = "Simulation: omitted trait and proxy control"
)
```


The simulation illustrates the proxy-control logic. When the true productive trait is observed, the Black coefficient is close to the true value. When the trait is omitted, the coefficient becomes too negative because the omitted trait is correlated with Black-student
status and affects grades. Adding an imperfect proxy moves the estimate back toward the oracle benchmark, but it does not fully solve the problem.

The empirical proxy exercise should therefore be read as a sensitivity check, not as proof that all relevant unobserved heterogeneity has been removed.

### 5.5 Behavioral and earlier-performance proxy blocks in the paper

Before turning to the empirical proxy model, we reload the data and define the control blocks used in this exercise. This makes the exercise self-contained.

We reload the data and reconstruct the richest OLS model from Exercise 4.

The paper uses several additional blocks to address the concern that teachers observe productive traits not fully captured by current scores, past grades, and family background.

The variables below are grouped by source and interpretation. This grouping matters because no single proxy perfectly measures the omitted productive attribute. The idea is instead to combine different imperfect pieces of information: earlier achievement-related indicators, parent reports, teacher- or school-related measures, and student self-reports.

Define the additional earlier-performance and behavioral proxy blocks.
